text.p: Ship repairer Hitachi Zosen Singapore Ltd is expanding shipbuilding capacity to complement its core ship repair business and sees no need for mergers to compete with local yards, a top official said on Tuesday.
"We are trying to engage more heavily on shipbuilding but shiprepair will still be our core business," executive chairman Takeshi Tenjin told Reuters in an interview.
He was unfazed by the proposed merger of two local yards -- Sembawang Corp Ltd and Jurong Shipyard Ltd.
The merged company would have more than half the market and nine dry docks, making it one of the world's largest repair firms. Tenjin said his strategy was different.
"The company's policy is not to be the biggest. Turnover is not our target but to provide good, quality services to our clients and grow from there," he said.

"I have no intention to merge or form alliances with anyone," he said, dispelling market rumours Hitachi, the smallest of the Big Four yards here, would need to merge to survive the keen competition in Singapore.
Ship repair now contributes 75-80 percent of the group's total revenue. But Tenjin said this would change once its Singapore $15 million berth extension was completed next week.
The extension of the slipway to 230 metres (250 yards) from 127 metres (139 yards) would allow the yard to build bulk carriers of up to 30,000 dwt.
Hitachi, a subsidiary of Osaka-based Hitachi Zosen Corp, is now engaged mainly in ship repair but has a building capacity for product carriers of 7,900-9,900 tonnes.

"When the slipway project is completed, ship repair will contribute about 60 percent while shipbuilding 35 percent," Tenjin said. The remaining five percent would come from industrial engineering-related businesses.
Tenjin said shipbuilding would complement a repair business subject to seasonal fluctuations. "Shipbuilding would blend with ship repair during the seasonal lull," he said.
Repair enquiries from oil and gas carriers, Hitachi's main customers, traditionally surge after mid-March to early October with January and February hitting the doldrums, Tenjin said.
Last year, Hitachi saw a dip in repair jobs to about 115 vessels from 155 previously, Tenjin said. However, he said unit price per ship improved slightly.
Its main customers comprised 25-30 percent Japanese shipowners, 30-40 percent European owners and the remaining from the region and the United States.
Tenjin was confident geography and infrastructure would ensure Signaproe's role as key ship repair centre, especially for tankers.
He dismissed concerns of challenges from other regional centres like Indonesia or the Philippines, where yards remain in infant developmental stages.
However, he did not dimiss the possibility of Hitachi looking for an alternative repair yard to Singapore due to rising labour costs.
